Stalk rot and ear rot (Fusarium spp.).

Symptoms: infected stalks turn brown internally and the pith can disintegrate, leaving a hollow, weakened stalk that is prone to lodging (falling over). On the ear, infected kernels develop a pinkish or salmon-coloured mould, often starting at the kernel tip and spreading; infected ears can show discoloured, shrunken kernels. This disease group is of particular concern because some Fusarium species can produce mycotoxins that are harmful to human and animal health if contaminated grain is consumed.

Management: prevention is the main strategy, since there is no cure once a plant is infected. Balanced fertilization (avoiding excess nitrogen, ensuring adequate potassium, since K deficiency increases susceptibility to stalk rot), avoiding drought stress, maintaining appropriate plant density, and harvesting promptly at maturity (rather than leaving mature grain exposed in the field for a long period) all help reduce risk. Resistant hybrids should be used where available.
